I'm testing whether the rule is about keeping shapes that repeat versus removing unique ones. In example 1, the repeated 3x3 blocks stay while irregular shapes get removed; in example 2 the plus shapes are kept but the 2x2 squares, despite appearing multiple times, get removed—so it's not simply about repetition count, there's something more specific going on with shape type.

Actually, maybe the pattern is about border-touching: shapes touching the edge of the grid get removed, while shapes fully interior are kept. Checking ex2, the removed squares (6, 4, 7) all touch the border, and in ex1 the removed 8-shape and 5-shape both touch an edge too, while the kept squares stay interior.

I try counting rectangle-family shapes together versus plus shapes, but that doesn't cleanly split either. Checking border-touching again for ex3 doesn't work, and symmetry doesn't hold up cleanly across examples either. The pattern that seems most promising is majority shape: in ex3 the H-shape appears three times while the full square appears once, so the rule may just be keep whichever shape is most common and remove the outlier.

I'm testing different hypotheses on what makes a shape survive: maybe it's not about shared border position or color repetition, but cell count. Checking example 2 again, the kept shapes have 5 cells while the removed ones have 4 or 6 cells — that might be the actual rule.

But then example 1 breaks it since the kept shape has 9 cells while removed ones have 6 and 8. Looking at example 3, colors 7 and 3 each appear twice, and the shape that repeats three times (the H shape in both colors) survives while the lone square shape gets removed — so frequency of shape type might matter more than color or cell count.

Since there's no test grid actually provided, I should just note that and ask for the held-out input before proceeding.
